justification_text:
At the time of the forecast, the point estimate for the one-day horizon of roughly 32.7 was anchored primarily to the most recent observed price or level, with only a small drift adjustment reflecting short-term momentum or mean-reversion tendencies. For the one-week estimate of 32.9, I incorporated a modest upward drift assumption, likely reflecting a slightly positive trend or carry effect visible in recent data, while keeping the adjustment conservative given the short horizon. The one-month estimate of 33.5 extended that drift further, compounding the weekly trend assumption over approximately four weeks. In all three cases, the point estimates are essentially a near-random-walk forecast with a small positive bias layered on top, which is a reasonable default when no strong structural signal dominates.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval of roughly 31.6 to 33.8 is relatively tight because there is limited time for new information or volatility to accumulate. By one week, the interval widens to 30.8–35.0, capturing a broader range of plausible paths as daily volatility has more sessions to compound. At one month, the interval stretches to 29.0–38.0, nearly nine units wide, because a month allows for meaningful trend shifts, macro surprises, or sentiment changes to materially move the level. The interval widths were calibrated using something close to a square-root-of-time scaling on an assumed daily or weekly volatility estimate, which is standard practice in the absence of regime-specific information.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected macroeconomic shock — such as a significant deterioration in economic data, a financial stability event, or a sharp risk-off episode — could drive the level well below 29.0 within a month. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as a policy announcement, better-than-expected fundamental data, or a broad risk-on rally could push the level above 38.0. Liquidity conditions and any scheduled high-impact events such as central bank decisions or major data releases within the forecast window are particular tail risks that the interval widths may not fully capture if those events land far from consensus expectations.

It is also worth noting that the intervals are stated at the 90% confidence level, meaning there is by construction a 10% probability of outcomes falling outside them even if the model is well-calibrated. In practice, financial and economic variables tend to have fatter tails than standard normal assumptions imply, so the true probability of an extreme outcome may be modestly higher than 10%.
